text: The con is small and repeatable: a woman lets an older man take her home, and by morning his money is gone and so is she. Nikki and Al have run it long enough that the routine has replaced most of the conversation between them, which is the interesting part: the crime is a job, and the job is what they have instead of a life. One dose goes wrong, and the road out gets emptier the further they take it, across country with few places for two people to be inconspicuous. Ninety-six minutes leaves no room for a plan, which suits a pair who never had one and would not agree on it now. What Bill Bennett keeps watching is the balance of trust between them, tilting a little each time one of them is left alone in a room with a stranger.

The house holds three generations, and the work that built it is running out. Timber runs on a longer clock than most trades, which is part of why a village organised around it comes apart slowly rather than all at once. Suzaku puts five people under that roof, a household of grandmother, son, wife, nephew and small daughter, and lets the economy press from outside the frame while the meals go on inside it. Naomi Kawase gives the situation ninety-five minutes and declines to raise her voice: the recession is never announced, and the development scheme meant to hold the valley together simply stops being mentioned. The Caméra d'Or went to it. What these five know about one another arrives in the pauses at the table rather than in anything said across it.

An advertising man dies, comes back, and concludes he is in Hell on the evidence that nothing whatsoever has changed. Same house, same accounts, same family, and a lengthening inventory of products that give people cancer, which he can now read as an itemised bill. Bliss commits to his reading and never winks at it, so the comedy has to be played straight: everyone else in the room is having an ordinary week. He starts writing notes to himself as proof of his own sanity, and the notes get worse. Ray Lawrence runs the premise 112 minutes without softening it into whimsy or hardening it into a lesson, which is a hard balance to hold that long. The wife, the daughter, the ex-prostitute he runs off with: each is a person with a schedule, not evidence for the case he is building.

Nineteen fifty-three, and a thirteen-year-old is delivered to a Catholic seminary to be made into something he has not yet agreed to be. The Devil's Playground gives the De La Salle Brothers who run the place the same weather as the boys they instruct: the men enforcing the rule are also serving it, and both sides of that wall are contending with the same appetite and the same doubt. Stories about religious schooling usually sort their people into a victim and a monster; Fred Schepisi keeps everyone inside one discipline and shows it working on them at different ages. It took the AACTA award for cinematography, which fits, since an institution is felt first as light, temperature, and rooms one may not leave. A hundred and seven minutes, and Tom Allen has years of this ahead of him.

Xiao Hong arrives on screen secondhand, assembled out of what other people remember about her, and their accounts do not agree. That choice costs Ann Hui the ordinary pleasures of biography: no single vantage, no settled verdict on the love affair, and no scene in which the writing gets explained. What it buys is a portrait of a writer as she was actually transmitted, through the men who loved her and the colleagues who read her. Nearly three hours, a great deal of it in transit: rooms taken for a season, cities left ahead of an army, a manuscript carried from one to the next. The war works on the film as pressure on an itinerary rather than as spectacle, and the affair is one more thing happening while she tries to get the writing done.

Tung is a policeman and Fai is a Triad, and they drink in the same places because the district is small and the arrangement is older than either of them. Beast Cops is more interested in maintaining that arrangement than in breaking it: who is owed a favour, which crimes get tolerated because the alternative is worse, how a street stays quiet on a Friday. Hong Kong's Best Film award went to a cop picture that spends much of its length on men loitering. Then Fai puts money on a rival, the hit goes wrong, and the equilibrium everyone has been feeding turns into a set of positions that have to be defended. Dante Lam Chiu-yin holds it at street level for 110 minutes, where loyalty is not a principle but a question of whose phone call gets answered at two in the morning.

The calendar is the obstacle: the death falls on a day when the rites cannot proceed, so the burial waits five days. Nora and her husband divorced after thirty years of marriage, and she has arranged things so that the funeral becomes his job, instructions included. Cinco días sin Nora counts those days out and stays with the logistics: a rabbi with rules, food that has to be dealt with, neighbours, a man who cannot decline a request he never accepted. Mariana Chenillo keeps to ninety-two minutes and finds the comedy in the arrangements, which is where the days after a death are actually spent. It took the Ariel for best picture. Nothing here argues for reconciliation; the film notes only how much of a marriage survives as knowledge of what the other person wanted done.

For some men a square joint is a moral fact, and the house going up is the argument. Three brothers in 1950s Queens quit a builder who cuts corners and start a company of their own, which sounds like the opening of a success story and turns out to be the opening of a family quarrel. The eldest learned the trade from their father and holds the others to a standard nobody asked him to enforce; they would like a wage and a Saturday. John Turturro directs at the speed of the work itself, and the two hours accumulate the way a build does, one stage at a time. Construction is taken seriously here as labour, with its own vocabulary of pride, and then that pride is refused the usual admiration: the man is right about the work and impossible in every room where the work is not.

The kung fu academy is a teahouse now, and the master whose name it was built on has spent thirty years unconscious. He wakes with the skills intact and the memories gone, into a block a developer wants cleared for flats. Gallants runs on that gap: a body kept in fighting condition for an occasion that stopped being scheduled, in a district that has quietly moved on from what it was for. Derek Kwok Chi-Kin plays this with affection rather than mockery, which matters, because a joke about old fighters can turn cruel in a second. Ninety-eight minutes, most of them at table height, in a room that spent an earlier life as a training hall. The coma does the accounting: three decades of change arrive at once, itemised, in one man's confusion.

Under occupation, most of the work of resistance turns out to be errands, carried out by people with day jobs. In Japanese-held Hong Kong a schoolteacher begins moving things across the city for people she is not supposed to know, and the man she was going to marry takes a different route on the same business. Ann Hui gives 130 minutes to what is actually available to civilians, which is unglamorous by design: a message carried by hand, a silence held at the wrong table, a class taught on time so that nothing looks unusual. The teaching continues throughout, and that continuity is the method rather than a pause in it. The guerrillas outside the city are armed and real, but the weight stays with the people who never left their district and had to price each week's risk against the household they were keeping.

Agent Chucho has played the Devil in his town's Nativity play for as long as anyone can remember, and the new pastor has just given the part to somebody else. He declines to accept the decision, and pursues the matter with the thoroughness he brings to his day job, which is where an eighty-eight-minute farce finds its engine. Emilio Portes plays it with a straight face, treating the Nativity play as the civic institution it is: a budget, a rehearsal schedule, factions with long memories. Christmas licenses the fantasy, and the fight stays parish-sized. What keeps this from being a sketch stretched to feature length is that the grievance is legible, since a man who is good at exactly one thing has been told, in front of everyone he knows, that he may no longer do it.

A musician keeps turning down the work that would pay him, which reads as principle for a few years and then begins to look like a habit he cannot afford. Hong Kong in 1993 had ample use for a composer willing to write what sells and none at all for one who will not. Best Film at the Hong Kong awards went to it: the industry it describes handing a prize to a story about refusing it. What alters the arithmetic is a young woman whose time is not open-ended, and who has no patience for a talent being held back as a bargaining position. Derek Yee Tung-Sing does not hedge the melodrama across 105 minutes: the feeling is played at full size, without apology, and the music is asked to carry the case rather than to decorate it.

Two years after the war a mining settlement near Vladivostok still holds Japanese prisoners nobody has sent home. The children who live there treat that as the ordinary condition of the world. Valerka and Galia make their entertainment out of whatever Suchan leaves lying about, and the games turn dangerous in the way of children nobody has time to supervise. Vitali Kanevsky films 1947 as a place at work rather than as a ruin, and the European prize for its production design registers something true: the mud has weight, the barracks have a temperature. What holds the picture together is its pitch, since the children shout, run, trade and turn on each other in ordinary childhood proportions while the catastrophe that put every adult around them there is never explained to them, or about them.

Shearing pays by the sheep, which makes the ranking in the shed arithmetic: everyone knows where they stand by lunchtime. Foley has been the fastest for years, and Black Arthur intends to take the position off him. The contest runs in a shed cut off from anything that is not shearing, where the same men drink together at night and get up before light to do it again. Then contractors bring in labour willing to work under the rate, and a private championship between two proud men shrinks beside a colder question about what a shed full of skilled hands is worth. Ken Hannam keeps the register dry, filming the work as work and at length, so the monotony is not a lapse in the portrait but a fair account of what these men are paid to absorb.
